In [[set theory]], a branch of [[mathematical logic]], '''Martin's maximum''', introduced by {{harvtxt|Foreman|Magidor|Shelah|1988}} and named after [[Donald A. Martin|Donald Martin]], is a stronger form of the [[proper forcing axiom]], itself a stronger form of [[Martin's axiom]].  It represents the broadest class of [[Forcing (mathematics)|forcings]] for which a forcing axiom is consistent.

Martin's maximum <math display=inline> (\operatorname{MM})</math> states that if ''D'' is a collection of <math>\aleph_1</math> dense subsets of a notion of forcing that preserves stationary subsets of ''ω''<sub>1</sub>, then there is a ''D''-generic filter. Forcing with a [[Countable chain condition|ccc]] notion of forcing preserves stationary subsets of ''ω''<sub>1</sub>, thus <math display=inline> \operatorname{MM}</math> extends <math display=inline> \operatorname{MA}(\aleph_1)</math>. If (''P'',≤) is not a stationary set preserving notion of forcing, i.e., there is a stationary subset of ''ω''<sub>1</sub>, which becomes nonstationary when forcing with (''P'',≤), then there is a collection ''D'' of <math>\aleph_1</math> dense subsets of (''P'',≤), such that there is no ''D''-generic filter. This is why <math display=inline> \operatorname{MM}</math> is called the maximal extension of Martin's axiom.

The existence of a [[supercompact cardinal]] implies the consistency of Martin's maximum.{{sfn|Jech|2003|p=684}} The proof uses [[Saharon Shelah|Shelah]]'s theories of semiproper forcing and iteration with revised countable supports.

<math display=inline> \operatorname{MM}</math> implies that the value of the [[cardinality of the continuum|continuum]] is <math>\aleph_2</math>{{sfn|Jech|2003|p=685}} and that the ideal of [[stationary set|nonstationary sets]] on ω<sub>1</sub> is <math>\aleph_2</math>-saturated.{{sfn|Jech|2003|p=687}} It further implies stationary reflection, i.e., if ''S'' is a stationary subset of some regular cardinal ''κ''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''ω''<sub>2</sub> and every element of ''S'' has countable cofinality, then there is an ordinal ''α''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''κ'' such that ''S''&nbsp;∩&nbsp;''α'' is stationary in&nbsp;''α''. In fact, ''S'' contains a closed subset of order type&nbsp;''ω''<sub>1</sub>.
